How It Works · Trucks

No Replacement for Displacement

GM's new 8.3-liter Duramax makes 1,230 lb-ft, the most of any pickup engine by GM's count. What's inside it, why GM made it bigger instead of working it harder, and what heavy-duty buyers are paying for with diesel at a record price.

By Sloane Whitaker · 11 minute read

Hot-rodders have a saying older than most of the trucks it gets quoted about: there's no replacement for displacement. Turbochargers, fuel injection and computers have spent 40 years proving it wrong. Engines kept getting smaller and making more power anyway.

On September 24, General Motors went the other way. The new Duramax turbo-diesel V8 for the 2027 Chevrolet Silverado HD and GMC Sierra HD grows from 6.6 liters to 8.3, and output jumps from 470 hp and 975 lb-ft to 555 hp and 1,230 lb-ft. Ford's best is 1,200 lb-ft. Ram's is 1,075.

It arrived in an awkward week to sell diesel. The national average reached a record $6.53 a gallon on September 22, according to AAA, against about $3.70 a year earlier. Here is what GM built, why it built it bigger, and who it is really for.

8.3 litersUp from 6.6 in the outgoing Duramax
555 hpUp from 470
1,230 lb-ftUp from 975. Ford's best is 1,200

What GM built

The 8.3 is a clean-sheet design, and GM says it is the first heavy-duty diesel V8 it has designed and built entirely on its own. The parts list reads more like a big rig's than a pickup's.

The block is compacted graphite iron. In ordinary gray iron, the graphite forms thin, sharp flakes that act like tiny cracks. In compacted graphite iron it forms short, blunt clumps, which makes the metal stronger and stiffer. GM says the new block is lighter than the gray iron it replaces.

The moving parts are forged: the crankshaft and the connecting rods. The pistons are steel, not aluminum. Steel keeps its strength at temperatures that soften aluminum, which is why the big diesels in semi trucks use it too.

The air comes through a variable-geometry turbocharger, whose vanes change angle so it behaves like a small turbo at low engine speed and a large one at high speed. A 2-stage air-to-water charge cooler then uses liquid coolant to chill that compressed air before it reaches the cylinders. Cooler air is denser, so more of it fits.

Everything downstream changed too: an upgraded exhaust brake, a new layout for the emissions hardware, and an Allison 10-speed automatic with new shift programming.

The trucks get their own firsts. GM says the new rack-and-pinion electric power steering is a first for heavy-duty pickups and gives about 30% more assist than the old hydraulic system. An electronic brake booster, 14.6-inch front rotors and 4-piston front calipers shorten stops by up to 20%, by GM's figures. The off-road ZR2 and Sierra AT4X add a Terrain Mode with one-pedal driving off road.

The ratings: up to 9,072 kg (20,000 lb) on a conventional hitch, 17,237 kg (38,000 lb) on a gooseneck, up from 16,329 kg (36,000 lb), and a gross combined weight rating of 21,092 kg (46,500 lb) for truck and trailer together. GM builds the engine at its DMAX plant in Brookville, Ohio, and the trucks reach dealers late this year. Prices haven't been announced.

Bigger, not harder

There are 2 ways to get more torque out of a diesel. You can make every liter work harder, with more boost, more fuel and more pressure in each cylinder. Or you can add liters.

Torque per liter shows which one an engine took, because it rises and falls with the average pressure inside the cylinders. That pressure is what an engineer means by how hard an engine is working. On that measure, the new Duramax and the one it replaces are almost identical.

Take the outgoing 6.6-liter's 975 lb-ft and scale it up by the new engine's extra displacement. You get 1,226 lb-ft. GM's published figure is 1,230.

Almost the entire gain is size.

Carveyance arithmetic: published peak torque divided by nominal displacement. Torque per liter tracks the average pressure in the cylinders, so a higher number means each liter is working harder. Sources: GM; Ford; Ram.

Ford took the other road. Its high-output 6.7-liter Power Stroke makes 1,200 lb-ft from 6.7 liters, about 21% more per liter than either Duramax. Ram's Cummins sits in between.

Why would GM choose size? It hasn't published boost or cylinder-pressure figures, so the answer here is general engineering, not inside information. A bigger engine can make the same output with each cylinder doing less. Lower peak pressure means less strain on the parts and less heat to get rid of, and heat matters most in exactly the job a heavy-duty truck is bought for: a full gooseneck trailer, a long grade, a hot afternoon. Heat is also the enemy of clean exhaust, because hotter combustion tends to make more nitrogen oxides.

The price of size is weight and space. GM hasn't said what the 8.3 weighs, and that is the number that decides how much payload the engine takes away.

The race to 1,230

Torque has become the number heavy-duty pickups fight over, and the Duramax shows how fast it has climbed. The first one, in 2001, made 520 lb-ft. The 8.3 makes 2.4 times that.

Ram was the first to reach 1,000 lb-ft in a pickup, with the high-output Cummins it showed in January 2019. Ford's high-output Power Stroke went to 1,200. GM now holds the number, for as long as these things last.

The torque title and the towing title aren't the same thing. Ford's F-450 is still rated to pull 18,144 kg (40,000 lb) on a gooseneck, more than the new GM. A tow rating is a judgment about the whole truck, including its frame, axles, brakes, cooling and hitch, not just the engine.

The 8.3 is also bigger than the biggest gasoline engine GM put in these trucks. The 8.1-liter big-block V8, sold in the Silverado and Sierra heavy-duty pickups from 2001, made at most 340 hp and 455 lb-ft. The new diesel makes 2.7 times that torque.

All GM, for the first time

The Duramax started as a partnership. GM and Isuzu formed DMAX in 1997 as a 60-40 joint venture to build diesel V8s in Moraine, Ohio, and the first Duramax went into GM's heavy-duty pickups in 2001. Isuzu sold its 40% to GM in 2022.

In June 2023 GM announced a $920 million expansion of the DMAX plant in Brookville, Ohio (about $1 billion in 2026 dollars). It is now a 1.4-million-square-foot site where machining and assembly happen under one roof, and it is where the 8.3 is built.

An engine like this stays in production for a long time. The 6.6-liter it replaces stayed in its final form, the L5P, from 2017 through 2026.

What the diesel costs, and what it buys

GM hasn't priced the 8.3. On the 2026 trucks, the 6.6-liter Duramax was a $10,825 option over the gasoline V8, the same on every 2500HD and 3500HD.

Nobody can tell you the 8.3's fuel economy either. Pickups with a gross vehicle weight rating above 3,856 kg (8,500 lb) are exempt from EPA fuel-economy labels, so heavy-duty trucks have no window-sticker mpg at all.

What can be worked out is the fuel itself. On September 28, AAA had diesel at $6.45 a gallon and regular at $4.48. At those prices a diesel has to go 44% farther on a gallon just to cost the same per mile as gasoline. A year earlier, with diesel around $3.70 and regular around $3.13, it needed to go 18% farther.

Carveyance arithmetic: the diesel price divided by the regular gasoline price. National averages from AAA. The efficiency range is the federal fueleconomy.gov estimate for diesel engines against similar gasoline engines.

The federal government's fuel-economy site puts diesel's edge over a similar gasoline engine at about 30% to 35%. A year ago that was a comfortable win. This fall it isn't enough.

An example: fuel cost for 15,000 miles a year
Gasoline truck, 10 mpgDiesel truck, 13.5 mpgDiesel's difference
Late September 2025$4,695$4,100Saves $595
September 28, 2026$6,720$7,167Costs $447 more

The mpg figures are an illustration, not ratings: the diesel is set 35% better, the top of the federal range. Heavy-duty trucks have no EPA ratings. Change the mpg and the dollars change, but the flip between the 2 years doesn't.

Even in the good year, the fuel savings in that example would take about 18 years to cover a $10,825 option. That has always been true of heavy-duty diesels, and their buyers know it. They pay for what happens with 9,072 kg (20,000 lb) behind the truck: strong torque at low engine speed, an exhaust brake that holds the load on the way down a grade, and higher tow ratings. A Ram 2500 is rated for up to 9,072 kg (20,000 lb) with the Cummins and 8,092 kg (17,840 lb) with the gasoline Hemi. Why diesel stopped being the cheap fuel is a story of its own, told in Diesel's Lost Advantage.

The trade-in risk

The usual case for the diesel option is that much of it comes back at trade-in. That depends on the price of fuel too. In 2008, the last time diesel spiked this fast, Black Book data showed 2005 to 2007 three-quarter-ton and one-ton diesel pickups losing nearly $6,000 in value (about $9,300 in 2026 dollars) between January and June. Their gasoline equivalents lost about $3,000 (about $4,650).

That isn't a forecast. It's a reminder that a used diesel is worth what the next buyer expects to pay at the pump.

Why GM did it anyway

From a gas station, an 8.3-liter diesel in a record-price month looks like poor timing. From a factory it looks different. The plant investment was announced in 2023, the engine was years in development, and if it lasts as long as the 6.6 it will still be in production long after this fall's prices are forgotten. A year ago, diesel cost about $3.70.

GM's wider truck plan points the same way. A week before the 8.3, it kept the 3.0-liter Duramax in the 2027 half-ton Silverado and Sierra and gave it a bigger fuel tank, while Ford leaned on hybrids and Ram on a range-extended truck. Diesel, Hybrid, or Generator? covers that split. In heavy-duty trucks nobody has blinked: Ford and Ram both still sell diesels, and GM just built the biggest one.

The people who buy these trucks tow for a living, or tow big things for fun: fifth-wheel campers, horse trailers, equipment. For them the question isn't whether diesel is cheap this month. It's whether the truck pulls the load up the grade without drama and stops it on the way down. That is the job GM built the 8.3 for.

The short version

The 8.3 gets its record torque by being bigger, not by working harder: per liter, it works no harder than the engine it replaces. That favors durability and heat control under load. At this fall's prices it won't pay for itself at the pump, and heavy-duty diesels rarely have.
